946.title: Paris, 1893
946.hook: he dies in a Paris hotel, far from home
946.howItsDone: Duleep Singh is buried at Elveden in Suffolk, and Sikh visitors to the churchyard remember him there; some Sikhs hold prayers for him and his mother at gatherings about the end of the kingdom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Duleep returns to Sikhi, and your line was he came back. What small step back did you take? Today, the end of the road for the man who came back. Day nine hundred forty-six.

A hotel room in Paris. Outside, the boulevards, the cafés, the noise of a great city. Inside, a man lies weak after a stroke, his body failing. He was born in Lahore. He sat on a throne as a child, lost it, grew up in a garden by the Ganges, lived as a gentleman in Suffolk, and came back to Sikhi in a port at Aden. Now he is here, in a rented room in a city that was never his home. Today: Paris.
screen: `A HOTEL ROOM IN PARIS.` → `A MAN WEAK AFTER A STROKE.` → `A CITY THAT WAS NEVER HOME.`

segments.voice: First, the wandering years. After Aden, Duleep Singh could not go to India and would not go back to his old life in England. He went to Paris. He tried to win support abroad for his claim to the Punjab, and even traveled to Russia in the hope of help. None came. His money ran low, his first wife died, and his health broke. Second, the letter. Late in his life, weakened, he wrote to Queen Victoria asking her pardon, and she forgave him. They met once more. It's a strange and tender scene: the Queen who held his diamond, and the Maharaja who had once fought her government with words. Third, the death. He died in a hotel in Paris, far from the Punjab and far from Elveden. His body was taken back to England and buried in the churchyard at Elveden, beside his wife and son, with a Christian service. He had come back to Sikhi, but he was not cremated with Sikh rites. For some who tell his story, that is one more thing taken from him. Fourth, a line for exiles. In a hymn of Guru Arjan in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru says that since he found the company of the holy, he has forgotten all envy of others; no one is his enemy and no one is a stranger, and he gets along with everyone. An exile is someone everywhere treats as a stranger. The Guru's line describes a company where nobody is one. Duleep Singh's life ended in a hotel room among strangers. So today's line reaches past him, to everyone far from home.
screen: `THE WANDERING YEARS.` · `A LETTER TO THE QUEEN.` · `A DEATH IN PARIS, A GRAVE IN SUFFOLK.` · `NO ONE A STRANGER.` · then, large: `FOR ALL EXILES.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for everyone far from home. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind people who are living somewhere that isn't home: refugees, migrants, students abroad, a neighbor who arrived last year, someone in a hospital or a prison. You don't need faces or names. Just hold them, all of them, in your mind for a while, without judging how they got there. If you pray, you can hold them before God, and say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Paris. The city where Duleep Singh, the boy king of the Punjab, died in a hotel room, far from the land he was born to rule. Today's word.
Your line: for all exiles. Today, hold all exiles in mind once, and do one kind thing for someone who is far from home. Day nine hundred forty-six.

947.title: Princess Sophia, suffragette
947.hook: Duleep's daughter Sophia campaigned for women's votes in Britain
947.howItsDone: Sikhs in Britain remember Princess Sophia Duleep Singh as a suffragette, and her story is often told alongside the Gurus' teaching that women and men are equal in the sangat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paris: Duleep Singh died in a hotel room far from Punjab, and your line was for all exiles. Who came to mind when you said it? Today, one of the children he left behind. Day nine hundred forty-seven.

Outside the gates of Hampton Court Palace, near London, a woman in a fine coat stands holding up a newspaper for sale. The paper is called The Suffragette. People walking past might know her face. She lives just across the road, in a grace-and-favor house the old Queen herself granted her. She is a goddaughter of Queen Victoria. Her father was the last Maharaja of the Sikh kingdom, the boy who lost a crown. And here she is on the pavement, selling a paper that demands the vote for women. Today: Princess Sophia.
screen: `A PRINCESS SELLING A NEWSPAPER.` → `A GODDAUGHTER OF THE QUEEN.` → `THE DAUGHTER OF DULEEP SINGH.`

segments.voice: First, the comfortable life. Sophia Duleep Singh grew up English in every outward way: country houses, ponies, dresses, and later a grace-and-favor home at Hampton Court. She could have stayed there quietly, and nobody would have blinked. Second, the turn. As her biographer Anita Anand tells it, a journey to India changed her. She saw Punjab, the land her father had ruled, and she saw people living under a government they had no voice in. Back in Britain, women had no vote either. She joined the women fighting for one, the suffragettes, and she didn't do it from the back row. Third, the march. She walked with the women who went to Parliament to demand the vote, on a day when the crowd was met with force. She refused to pay her taxes, saying in effect: no vote, no tax. So officials seized her things, jewelry among them, and sold them at auction, and the fight went on. Fourth, the old line underneath it. Guru Nanak, in the Asa di Var, asks why anyone would speak ill of woman, when it is from woman that kings themselves are born. Sophia was raised far from the Gurus' hymns, and nobody can say how much of them she knew. But a daughter of the Sikh royal house stood in the street for women's equal voice, and the old line and the new march sound alike. That's today's word.

segments.voice: Two minutes with a fair cause. Sit comfortably, and let your breath slow down. Bring to mind one cause you think is fair, large or small: a neighbor who isn't being heard, a rule at work that falls hard on some people, a question of who gets a say. Don't argue it out. Just hold it. Now ask: what is one small, peaceful thing I could actually do for it this week? A signature, a phone call, a word in a meeting. Let one answer come. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Princess Sophia. Sophia Duleep Singh, daughter of the last Maharaja, goddaughter of a queen, who marched and refused her taxes for women's right to vote. Today's word.

948.title: Princess Bamba
948.hook: another daughter moved to Lahore and kept the family's memory
948.howItsDone: Visitors to the Lahore Fort can see the Princess Bamba Collection of Sikh-era paintings and objects, and some Sikh families keep their own memory of the Sikh kingdom in pictures, stories and visits to Lahore.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Princess Sophia at the palace gates, and your line was the princess marched. Did you take a step for a fair cause? Today, her older sister, who went the other way: east. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

A house in Lahore, full of old things. Paintings of men in turbans and jewels. Small portraits on ivory. Pieces of a vanished court, gathered one by one and kept in a city this family once ruled. The woman who gathered them was born in England, raised English, and could have stayed there all her life. Instead she moved to Lahore, the capital her grandfather Ranjit Singh had ruled, and her father had lost as a boy. Today: Princess Bamba.
screen: `A HOUSE FULL OF OLD PORTRAITS.` → `BORN IN ENGLAND.` → `SHE MOVED TO LAHORE.`

segments.voice: First, who she was. Bamba Duleep Singh was Duleep Singh's eldest daughter, Sophia's sister. Like Sophia, she grew up in English houses, far from Punjab, with a father who had been taken from it. Second, the move. She traveled to Punjab, and in the end she stayed. She married a doctor who taught at the medical college in Lahore, and made her home in the old capital. For a child of an exiled family, that was a quiet kind of return: not to a throne, but to a street, a house, a city. Third, the keeping. Over the years she gathered what she could of her family's past: paintings, portraits, objects from Ranjit Singh's court. After she died, the collection she kept passed into the care of the government in Lahore, and today it is known by her name, the Princess Bamba Collection, held at the Lahore Fort. A kingdom was gone. Its rooms had emptied. And one granddaughter set about gathering up what was left. Fourth, the Sikh word nearby. The Gurus use the word simran for remembering: holding the Name of God in mind, again and again, so it isn't lost. What Bamba did is not simran in that sense. Her remembering was of a family and a court. But the two share a shape: memory is not something that simply stays. Somebody keeps it, or it goes. Bamba died in Lahore and is buried there, in the city her family once ruled. That's today's word.
screen: `DULEEP SINGH'S ELDEST DAUGHTER.` · `A QUIET RETURN TO LAHORE.` · `THE PRINCESS BAMBA COLLECTION.` · `MEMORY HAS TO BE KEPT.` · then, large: `SHE KEPT THE MEMORY.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for a family memory. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind one thing from your family that could easily be lost: a recipe, a saying, a story about a grandparent, a photo in a drawer, a song somebody hummed. Hold it in your mind and look at it closely, the way Bamba might have held a portrait. Who else knows this? If nobody does, it's yours to keep. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Princess Bamba. Bamba Duleep Singh, Duleep's eldest daughter, who made her home in Lahore and gathered her family's past into a collection that bears her name. Today's word.
Your line: she kept the memory. Today, keep one family memory on purpose: write it down, ask about it, or tell it to someone younger. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

949.title: Sikh soldiers under the Raj
949.hook: after the great rising against Company rule, the British recruited Sikhs heavily into the army
949.howItsDone: Sikh regiments have kept the Guru Granth Sahib with them, read by a regimental granthi, and Sikh families remember soldier ancestors who served overseas in the British Indian Army.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Princess Bamba in Lahore, and your line was she kept the memory. Which family memory did you keep? Today we leave the royal family and follow ordinary Sikh men into uniform. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

A barracks at dawn, somewhere a very long way from Punjab. A hot port, a cold frontier, a city where nobody speaks Punjabi. Rows of young men tie their turbans before parade. In one room, set apart, a granthi opens the Guru Granth Sahib and reads the morning's hymn. These soldiers wear the uniform of the British Crown. Not long before, men from the same villages had fought the British at Ferozeshah and Sobraon. Today: Sikh soldiers under the Raj.
screen: `TURBANS TIED BEFORE PARADE.` → `THE GURU IN THE BARRACKS.` → `ONCE ENEMIES, NOW RECRUITS.`

segments.voice: First, the switch. After the wars and the annexation, the British army in India was shaken by a great rising against Company rule. Punjab did not join it in strength, and Sikh soldiers fought on the British side. After that, the British looked to Punjab for soldiers, and Sikhs were recruited heavily. Second, the uniform. British officers came to call Sikhs a martial race, a label about whole peoples that historians now treat with care. And the army wanted its Sikh soldiers to look like Khalsa Sikhs: uncut hair, the turban, the outward form. Some histories argue that this helped keep the Khalsa form strong in villages at a time when it might have faded. Third, the Guru went too. Sikh regiments carried the Guru Granth Sahib with them, with a granthi to read it, so a soldier posted far from home could still hear the hymns in the morning. Service took these men to garrisons and battlefields across the empire, far from wives, parents and fields. Fourth, a line about where the Guru sits. In a hymn of Guru Ram Das in Raag Asa, the Guru says that wherever the true Guru goes and sits, that place is made beautiful. A barracks room far from Punjab, with the Guru Granth Sahib open in it, could be read that way. But the uniform belonged to a foreign Crown, and Sikhs still talk about what that meant: honor, a living for poor families, and a hard question about whose battles they were fighting. That's today's word.

Sikh soldiers under the Raj. Sikh men recruited into the British army after the kingdom fell, keeping the Khalsa form and the Guru's hymns in barracks across the empire. Today's word.

950.title: Canal colonies
950.hook: new canals turned dry land green and Sikh farmers moved west to farm it
950.howItsDone: Sikh families from the old canal colonies of western Punjab still tell stories of the villages their grandparents built there, and Sikhs who recite the Japji in the morning end it with the salok that names water as the father.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sikh soldiers under the Raj, and your line was far-off service. Did you reach someone far from home? Today, the men who stayed with the land, and a land that moved under them. Day nine hundred fifty.

Dry ground, cracked and pale, with thorny scrub and not much else. Herders cross it with their animals. Rain is rare. Then a channel of water arrives, cut straight across the plain, and the ground on either side darkens. Within a few seasons there is wheat where there was dust, and a family from a crowded village in central Punjab is standing in a field that, a few years before, was nobody's farm at all. Today: canal colonies.
screen: `DRY GROUND AND THORNY SCRUB.` → `A CHANNEL OF WATER ARRIVES.` → `WHEAT WHERE THERE WAS DUST.`

segments.voice: First, the canals. In western Punjab, between the rivers, lay wide dry uplands that people called the bar. British engineers dug canals from the rivers across this land, and where the water went, farms could grow. Second, the settlers. The government granted the new land to families brought in from other parts of Punjab, and Sikh farmers were among them, leaving crowded home villages for bigger plots out west. They built houses, wells, and gurdwaras, and whole new villages grew up around the canals. Third, the towns. New market towns were laid out to serve the colonies. One of them, Lyallpur, was planned with bazaars running out from a clock tower at its center. Today that city lies in Pakistan, and how Sikh families left these lands is a later, harder story. For now, it was a story of water and wheat. Fourth, what the Gurus said about water. The salok at the close of the Japji names the world as a family: air is the Guru, water is the father, and the great earth is the mother. In the colonies, farmers could watch that line take shape: water making fields out of dust. No crop grew on that plain until the water came, and a farmer's whole year hung on the canal running on time. That's today's word.
screen: `CANALS ACROSS THE DRY BAR.` · `SETTLERS FROM CENTRAL PUNJAB.` · `A TOWN AROUND A CLOCK TOWER.` · `WATER IS THE FATHER.` · then, large: `WATER MADE FIELDS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with water. If you can, look at some water right now: a glass on the table, a tap, rain on a window, a river from a bridge. If you can't, picture the last water you saw. Sit, and breathe. Follow it back in your mind: where did it come from before it reached you? A reservoir, a pipe, a cloud, a river. Think of the fields it might have passed on the way. Let yourself feel the size of it for a moment. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Canal colonies. Dry land in western Punjab, watered by new canals and settled by farming families, Sikhs among them, who built villages, wells and gurdwaras there. Today's word.

951.title: Missionaries and debates
951.hook: Christian missions and new Hindu reform groups debated with Sikhs over identity
951.howItsDone: Sikh histories describe the late nineteenth century as a time of public debate in Punjab, when Sikhs founded presses, newspapers and societies to explain their faith; Sikhs read Guru Nanak's Sidh Gosht as a model of question and answer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the canal colonies, and your line was water made fields. Did you stop before a glass of water? Today, Punjab gets noisy: preachers, presses and arguments. Day nine hundred fifty-one.

A crowded bazaar in a Punjab town. On a wooden platform, a preacher is speaking about his faith, and a small crowd has gathered. Across the street, a printing press is turning out pamphlets in Punjabi and Urdu, some of them arguing with the preacher, some arguing with each other. In a schoolroom nearby, a teacher is telling Sikh boys a story about who their Gurus were, and it isn't the story their grandmothers told. Everybody has an answer to the same question: what are the Sikhs? Today: missionaries and debates.
screen: `A PREACHER IN THE BAZAAR.` → `PRESSES TURNING OUT PAMPHLETS.` → `WHAT ARE THE SIKHS?`

segments.voice: First, the missions. With British rule came Christian missionaries. They opened schools and hospitals, printed books, and preached in towns and bazaars. Some Sikhs studied in their schools, and a few became Christians, and each conversion was felt in the wider community. Second, the reformers. In the same years a Hindu reform movement, the Arya Samaj, grew strong in Punjab, calling people back to the Vedas and opening schools of its own. Some of its writing spoke harshly of the Sikh Gurus, and Sikh writers answered that it struck at who they were. Third, the debates. Punjab filled with public meetings, newspapers and pamphlets. Christians, Arya Samajis, Muslims, Sikhs: each wrote, each answered, and the arguments could be sharp. Sikhs set up presses and societies to answer in print, and to teach their own history in their own words. Fourth, the Guru's way of arguing. Guru Nanak had faced hard questions too. In the Sidh Gosht, the Guru Granth Sahib records a long conversation with the yogis: they ask, he answers, they ask again, and the whole thing moves by question and reply rather than shouting. And in another hymn Guru Nanak says that, as long as we live in this world, we should listen to some and say some. In the Guru's line, the listening comes before the saying. That's today's word.
screen: `SCHOOLS, PRESSES AND PREACHING.` · `A HINDU REFORM MOVEMENT GROWS.` · `PAMPHLETS ANSWERING PAMPHLETS.` · `LISTEN TO SOME, SAY SOME.` · then, large: `CALM IN DEBATE.`

Missionaries and debates. Christian missions and Hindu reform groups in British Punjab, and the Sikhs who answered them with presses, schools and argument. Today's word.

952.title: The keepers of the gurdwaras
952.hook: hereditary keepers treated gurdwaras as private property
952.howItsDone: Sikh histories remember the era of the mahants as the background to the gurdwara reform movement, and they also honor the Udasi custodians who kept gurdwaras open in hard times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, missionaries and debates, and your line was calm in debate. Did you listen all the way to the end? Today ends a week that ran from Paris to Punjab's own gurdwaras. Day nine hundred fifty-two.

A gurdwara door, and a man with the keys. He didn't build the gurdwara. The sangat didn't choose him. He holds the keys because his teacher held them before him, and his teacher's teacher before that. The offerings that pilgrims leave go into his keeping. The land around the shrine is written in his name. If the sangat doesn't like how he runs it, there isn't much they can do. Today's word is his title: mahant.
screen: `A MAN WITH THE KEYS.` → `HANDED DOWN, NOT CHOSEN.` → `MAHANT.`

segments.voice: First, where the keepers came from. A mahant is the head of a religious house, a title used beyond the Sikh tradition too. Sikh histories say that in hard years, when Khalsa Sikhs were hunted and often far from home, gurdwaras were looked after by custodians, among them Udasis, an order of ascetics who honor Guru Nanak. Thanks to them, doors stayed open. Second, how it hardened. The keeping passed from teacher to chosen disciple, or father to son. Under British rule the courts tended to treat the shrine and its land as the mahant's own property. What had been a trust began to look like an estate. Third, what went wrong. Some mahants, not all, lived well on the offerings and ran the gurdwaras as they pleased. Reformers complained of practices in some shrines that they said went against the Gurus' teaching, and of a sangat with no say over its own house of worship. Fourth, the Gurus on what belongs to others. Guru Nanak says that taking what rightly belongs to another is as forbidden as the food a person's own faith forbids. A gurdwara belongs to the sangat. When one man holds it as his own, something shared has slipped into private hands. And looking back on this week: an exile dying in Paris, a princess marching, a princess keeping memory, soldiers far away, farmers on new land, Punjab arguing with itself, and now the keys of the gurdwaras held in a few private hands. A people without a kingdom, asking what was still theirs. That's today's word.
screen: `KEEPERS IN HARD YEARS.` · `A TRUST TURNS INTO AN ESTATE.` · `SOME MAHANTS, NOT ALL.` · `THE GURDWARA BELONGS TO THE SANGAT.` · then, large: `SHARED THINGS NEED CARE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with something shared. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing that belongs to more than one person: a park, a shared kitchen, a family home, a community hall, a group's money, a tradition. Ask quietly: who actually holds it? Who has the keys, who makes the decisions, who cleans up? Is that how it should be? Don't fix anything yet. Just see it clearly. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Mahant. The head of a religious house; in Sikh history, a hereditary keeper of a gurdwara, some of whom came to treat the shrine as their own. Today's word.
Your line: shared things need care. Today, take care of one shared thing you usually leave to someone else: wipe the counter, refill the jug, tidy the space. Day nine hundred fifty-two.

fork.setup: you're in the sangat of a gurdwara. the mahant keeps the offerings and runs things as he pleases, and the land is in his name. what can you do, at this point in the story?
options: vote him out at the next meeting.
very little, because the law treats the shrine as his.
take the keys by force.
fork.reveal: the courts tended to back the mahant's claim. changing that would take a long reform struggle, which comes later in the story.

original.note: mahant, the head of a religious house; a title used beyond the Sikh tradition too.

trapdoor: what you thought: gurdwaras have always been run by committees of the sangat.
what it means: for a long time, gurdwaras were held by hereditary keepers, mahants, who passed the keys down.
what a scholar hears: custodians, often Udasis, kept shrines open in hard years; under British law the shrine and its land came to be treated as the mahant's estate.
